newsitem.title: EU: OPINION - The prospects for pension funds after EM.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - The prospects for pension funds after EM.

text.p: By Koen de Ryck, permanent representative of the European Federation for Retirement Provision, the body which represents pension funds in the European Union.

The arrival of the single currency and the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on January 1, 1999 are creating new expectations that a EU-wide pensions policy can finally get off the ground.

In the past the European Commission was not able to get pensions reform, particularly related to the funded pillar, past European finance ministers. The irony is that countries such as France, Germany, Italy and Spain, which are most in need of reform because their state pension promises exceed what they can deliver and are a drag an their public budgets, were also the least co-operative with the Commission's initiatives.

This is all quickly changing now. Whereas pensions and particularly state pensions were a quasi taboo subject until recently, awareness of the need for change is growing by the second, particularly in the above mentioned countries which were so opposed to the proposals of the Commission.

There is hope, even quasi-certainty, that pensions will be much higher on the political agendas as from now on and the Commission was right, in our view, to take up the matter again and to engage in the writing of a Green Paper which will be issued in the very near future and which will be backed by the three Commissioners who are in charge of all aspects which englobe pensions. That is the Internal Market, Financial Institutions and Taxation Commissioner Mario Monti; Economic and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy; and Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn.

The Green Paper is therefore expected to have a significant impact and political weight which is all the more important because the Commission, after consultation, refining and after having located areas where progress can be made, will have "to sell" the Green Paper and new policy initiatives to the highest political, employer and trade union levels in the member states.

The Green Paper is expected to offer a thorough analysis of the highly complicated and widely differing pension systems throughout the Union, particularly related to the second Pillar -- that is the pillar of hitherto essentially voluntary provision on group levels above the state/social security first pillar provision.

It will, we expect, make an inventory of where we differ between countries and systems and of what we have in common. It will ask questions on a whole series of subject matters which will give the industry i-e. the pension funds; the insurance companies; the banks; the investment funds; the money managers and all other interested parties an opportunity to respond. This will permit the Commission to define in which areas progress can be made and to come out with appropriate policy initiatives whether by directives, by recommendations or by communications.

This is not one minute too early because pensions are no doubt an area where progress is vital since they affect all EU citizens and the economy i.e. economic growth and therefore indirectly job creation and capital markets.
Not reforming pensions could lead to disruption and could seriously destabilise all previous and future painful efforts to successfully introduce the EMU and to make it an enduring success.

Pensions are far more important than the euro as they affect everybody sooner or later in their standard of living. Europe has performed poorly in terms of economic growth and employment. It has adapted insufficiently to the glabalisation of our economies and to the shifts in global competitiveness.

The euro, although an important objective by itself, is no panacea for higher growth and less unemployment like Mr. Hans Tietmeyer, the Chairman of the Bundesbank, recently said. There is a need to be realistic, Mr. Tietmeyer said, and to set the level of social protection in proportion to what is financially possible without endangering competitiveness.

Pensions, with exceptions notably in the United Kingdom, The Netherlands, Ireland and Denmark where well funded systems complement state provisions, are increasingly perceived as a burden which risks to jeopardise the necessary equilibrium between growth, intergenerational fairness and social protection, a model of which most Europeans are proud but which is increasingly difficult to sustain.

Pensions are big numbers in terms of people, liabilities and for the lucky ones, assets. They are no doubt our "biggest challenge" of the near future and they have been neglected, relatively spoken, for too long. They now impose themselves and they can no longer be avoided as a matter of the highest priority EU-wide.

Countries have a choice, they can either try to dump the subject further, in which case they will only inflict harm on themselves and get poorer, even risk to be thrown out of the EMU or never get in, or they can see pensions as their "biggest opportunity" to sustain the standard of living of the retired population, to develop their capital markets and by so doing to support economic growth, competitiveness and job creation, like Asian, Latin American and Eastern European countries facing the same problem are now doing quicker and more successfully than EU member states, with exceptions.

There is far too much reliance on pay-as-you-ga (PAYG) schemes in the EU and a partial shift to funding is necessary. This could be mandatory in the first pillar, with total freedom of investment and open competition among providers of investment and other services. The chances for this to succeed are not good. Would governments have the discipline not to oblige these assets to be invested solely in public debt, which would merely replace pension liabilities by debt reimbursement obligations for future generations, or worse would they not sacrifice the funded part to other priorities as soon as budget pressures occur ?

Or it can be done in the second pillar, either mandatorily with a low minimum funding requirement and a possibility to finance more and to differentiate, or voluntarily with the same freedom of investment and more certainty for participants governments will not lay their hand on these reserves.

If the voluntary systems raise coverage i.e. the number of participants and generate sufficient assets which are optimally invested there is a chance to provide better pensions at the lowest possible cost -- capital markets do wonders -- for more people and to decrease pressure an state schemes which in any case need to be maintained to offer a first pillar of social protection, in full solidarity for everybody in need of this.

The unavoidable retrenchment of first pillar pensions, which will entail a reduction of benefits, if bankruptcy of this system is to be avoided, necessitates all the more the strengthening of the second pillar. Funding in the second pillar i.e. group solidarity (particularly with Defined Benefit type plans and/or individual responsibility (particularly with Defined Contribution type plans) combined with PAYG financing in the first pillar diversifies the pensions financing risk and makes us less vulnerable to ageing. In other words, funded plans will help to assure a sufficient income replacement level for the retired and will be necessary for the survival of PAYG schemes.

A reform of pensions in that direction is likely to have positive effects on the quality of aggregate savings i.e. not necessarily over the longer term more savings but better savings/investments because savings will be institutionalised and more professionally invested which offers far reaching effects for capital market expansion, transparency, liquidity and corporate governance.

There should be no doubt that the EMU will put the whole unfunded pensions liabilities financing problem in the forefront. Contribution rates can hardly be increased nor can retirement ages be further reduced. Something will have to give in and that process has already started. Governments are already retrenching on state pension promises and benefits are being reduced. The first wave of measures has already passed and is slowly and gradually implemented to avoid resistance. More, much more will have to follow. Are governments going to borrow themselves out of the pensions dilemma or are they going to demonstrate discipline and imagination to build a better and stronger second pillar before it is too late ?

There is no doubt in our mind that the rating agencies for public and other debt issues, after the introduction of the euro, will focus on the general government sector including local and regional governments as well as on social security liabilities of which PAYG and budgetary pensions (for civil servants) are the largest part and that contingent liabilities and pension obligations will assume greater importance in the ratings they will apply.

That will separate those who neglect their pension liabilities quickly from those with discipline through the interest rate mechanism. Too bad for those who take less care, their populations will pay a high price (higher taxes; higher contributions; higher interest rates; less growth; less jobs) but worse, they will destabilise the well functioning of the EMU itself.

Governments can, of course, retrench further before or after the budgetary impact becomes unsustainable. Apart from the United Kngdom, The Netherlands, Ireland and Denmark that is what is likely to happen in most other EU member states. It could create enormous tensions because the populations have greater expectations than what can be delivered. The electoral risks are great but far more important is the risk of no change and of further destroying economic growth and wealth creation for the whole population.

There are sign that things are changing for the better as the recent, admittedly modest, moves to a funded pillar an top of PAYG in France and Italy, two nations with excessive PAYG promises, are demonstrating and that gives hope. The Commission's Green Paper also brings hope for the funded pillar that finally, not one minute too early, new EU-wide policy initiatives, with due respect for local subsidiarity, can be developed.
